source_text: Ergo, inquiunt, si Christus non homo est tantum sed et deus, Christum autem refert scriptura mortuum pro nobis et resuscitatum, iam docet nos scriptura credere deum mortuum: aut si deus non moritur, Christus autem mortuus refertur, non erit Christus deus, quoniam deus non potest accipi mortuus. si umquam intellegerent aut intellexissent quod legunt, numquam tam periculose omnino loquerentur. sed erroris semper est abrupta dementia; et non est nouum si usque ad periculosa descendunt, qui fidem legitimam reliquerunt. si enim scriptura proponeret Christum tantummodo deum, et nulla in illo fragilitatis humanae sociatio esset permixta, merito illorum hic aliquid ualuisset sermo contortus, ‘si Christus deus, Christus autem mortuus, ergo mortuus est deus.’ sed cum non tantummodo illum, ut ostendimus iam frequenter, deum sed et hominem scriptura constituat, consequens est, quod immortale est, incorruptum mansisse teneatur. quis enim non intellegat, quod impassibilis sit diuinitas, passibilis uero sit humana fragilitas? cum ergo tam ex eo quod deus est, quam etiam ex illo quod homo est, Christus intellegatur esse permixtus et esse sociatus,—verbum enim caro factum est, et habitauit in nobis—quis non sine ullo magistro atque interprete ex sese facile cognoscat, non illud in Christo mortuum esse quod deus est, sed illud in illo mortuum esse quod homo est? quid enim si diuinitas in Christo non moritur, sed carnis solius substantia exstinguitur, quando et in ceteris hominibus, qui non sunt caro tantummodo, sed caro et anima, caro quidem sola incursum interitus mortisque patiatur, extra leges autem interitus et mortis anima incorrupta cernatur? hoc enim et ipse dominus, hortans nos ad martyrium et ad contemptum omnis humanae potestatis, aiebat: ne timueritis eos qui corpus occidunt, animam autem occidere non possunt. quod si anima immortalis occidi aut interfici non potest in quouis alio, licet corpus et caro sola possit interfici, quanto magis utique uerbum dei deus in Christo interfici omnino non potuit, cum caro sola et corpus occisum sit? si enim hanc habet generositatem immortalitatis anima in quouis homine, ut non possit interfici, multo magis hanc habet potestatem generositas uerbi dei, ut non possit occidi. nam si potestas hominum ad interficiendam sacram dei potestatem, et si crudelitas humana ad interficiendam animam deficit, multo magis ad dei uerbum interficiendum deficere debebit. nam cum ipsa anima, quae per dei uerbum facta est, ab hominibus non occiditur, multo magis utique uerbum dei perimi non posse credetur. et si plus non potest hominum cruenta saeuitia aduersus homines, quam ut tantummodo corpus occidat, quanto magis utique in Christo non ualebit, quam ut item tantummodo corpus occidat: ut, dum per haec colligitur non nisi hominem in Christo interfectum, appareat ad mortalitatem sermonem in loco non esse deductum. nam si Abraham, et Isaac, et Iacob, quos homines tantummodo constat fuisse, manifestum est uiuere—ommnes enim, inquit, illi uiuunt deo, nec mors in illis animam perimit, quae corpora ipsa soluit; ius enim suum exercere potuit in corpora, in animas exercere non ualuit: aliud enim in illis mortale, et ideo mortuum, aliud in illis immortale, et ideo intellegitur non exstinctum, ob quam causam uiuere deo pronuntiati et dicti sunt,—multo magis utique mors in Christum aduersum solam materiam corporis potuit ualere, aduersus diuinitatem sermonis non potuit se exercere. frangitur enim potestas mortis, ubi intercedit auctoritas immortalitatis.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, they say, if Christ is not only human but also God, and yet Scripture reports that Christ died and was resurrected for us, then Scripture teaches us to believe that God died. Alternatively, if God cannot die, but Christ is reported to have died, then Christ will not be God, because God cannot be taken to have died. If they ever understood or had understood what they read, they would never speak so perilously. But error is always marked by abrupt madness, and it is not new for those who have abandoned legitimate faith to descend into perilous territory. For if Scripture presented Christ as only God, with no association of human fragility, their twisted argument might have some merit: 'If Christ is God, and Christ died, then God died.' However, since Scripture constitutes Christ not only as God, as we have frequently shown, but also as human, it follows that what is immortal and incorrupt remains so. Who does not understand that divinity is impassible, while human fragility is passible? Since Christ is understood to be a mixture and association of both God and human, as the Word became flesh and dwelled among us, who cannot easily recognize without any teacher or interpreter that it was not the divine aspect that died in Christ, but the human aspect? What if divinity in Christ does not die, but only the substance of flesh is extinguished, just as in other humans who are not only flesh but also flesh and soul, the flesh alone suffers the onset of death, while the incorrupt soul remains outside the laws of death? The Lord himself, encouraging us to martyrdom and contempt for all human power, said: 'Do not fear those who kill the body, but cannot kill the soul.' If the immortal soul cannot be killed or destroyed in anyone else, although the body and flesh alone can be killed, how much more certainly can the Word of God, who is God in Christ, not be killed, since only the flesh and body were killed? If the soul, which was made through the Word of God, has the generosity of immortality in any human, so that it cannot be killed, how much more does the Word of God have the power not to be killed. For if human power and cruelty are insufficient to kill the sacred power of God and the soul, they will be even more insufficient to kill the Word of God. Since the soul, which was made through the Word of God, is not killed by humans, it is even more believable that the Word of God cannot be destroyed. And if human cruelty can do no more than kill the body, how much more will it not prevail in Christ to do only the same, killing only the body, so that it is clear that only the human aspect was killed in Christ, and the argument about mortality is not applicable. For if Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who were only human, are said to be alive, since all of them live for God, and death does not destroy their souls, which only separate their bodies, because God could exercise his power over their bodies but not over their souls, and what is mortal in them has died, while what is immortal is understood not to be extinguished, for which reason they are said to live for God, then death could prevail against Christ only in regard to the material body, but not against the divinity of the Word. The power of death is broken when the authority of immortality intervenes.

pass_b_english: So they claim: if Christ is not only human but also God, and yet Scripture reports that Christ died and was raised for us, then Scripture teaches us to believe that God died. Or if God cannot die, but Christ is reported to have died, then Christ will not be God, because God cannot be taken to have died. If they ever understood or had understood what they read, they would never speak so perilously. But error is always marked by abrupt madness, and it is nothing new for those who have abandoned the legitimate faith to descend into such perilous territory. For if Scripture presented Christ as only God, with no association of human fragility mixed in, their twisted argument might have some merit: 'If Christ is God, and Christ died, then God died.' However, since Scripture constitutes Christ not only as God, as we have frequently shown, but also as human, it follows that what is immortal must remain incorrupt. Who does not understand that divinity is impassible, while human fragility is passible? Since Christ is understood to be a mixture and association of both the divine and the human—for the Word became flesh and dwelled among us (John 1:14)—who cannot easily recognize without any teacher or interpreter that it was not the divine element that died in Christ, but the human element? What if divinity in Christ does not die, but only the substance of flesh is extinguished, just as in other humans who are not only flesh but flesh and soul, the flesh alone suffers the onset of death, while the incorrupt soul remains outside the laws of death? The Lord himself said this, encouraging us to martyrdom and contempt for all human power: 'Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul' (Matthew 10:28). If the immortal soul cannot be killed or destroyed in anyone else, although the body and flesh alone can be killed, how much more certainly could the Word of God, who is God in Christ, not be killed, since only the flesh and body were killed? If the soul has the generosity of immortality in every human, so that it cannot be killed—since it was made through the Word of God—how much more does the generosity of the Word of God have the power not to be killed. For if human power and cruelty are insufficient to kill the sacred power of God and the soul, they will be even more insufficient to kill the Word of God. Since the soul, which was made through the Word of God, is not killed by humans, it is even more believable that the Word of God cannot be destroyed. And if human cruelty can do no more than kill the body, how much more will it not prevail in Christ to do only the same, killing only the body, so that it is clear that only the human aspect was killed in Christ, and the argument about mortality is not applicable. For if Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who were only human, are shown to be alive—for all of them live for God, and death does not destroy their souls, which only release their bodies; for death could exercise its right over their bodies, but not over their souls: one thing in them was mortal, and so it died; another was immortal, and so it is understood not to be extinguished, for which reason they are declared and said to live for God—then how much more certainly could death prevail against Christ only with regard to the material of the body, but could not exercise itself against the divinity of the Word. For the power of death is broken where the authority of immortality intervenes.
